newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Debtors' strike may cut Colombian coffee output.
newsitem.headline: Debtors' strike may cut Colombian coffee output.

text.p: The debtors' strike declared by Colombia's independent coffee growers Wednesday could support an overall trend toward lower output from the world's second-largest coffee producer, industry sources said.

They said it was still too soon to say whether members of the country's leading independent coffee growers' association, Unidad Cafetera Nacional, would make good on their pledge to withhold payments on all past-due loans.

But if they do, Deputy Agriculture Minister Jairo Bernando Arias said banks may have no choice but to foreclose on mortgages and seize control of what the UCN says are about 50,000 plantations whose owners already face legal problems because of outstanding debts.

That, in turn, could lead to the abandonment of a large number of coffee farms and contribute to what Colombia's Roman Catholic church described this week as a mass exodus of peasants from the guerrilla war and grueling poverty ravaging rural Colombia.
Production of numerous agricultural products has dropped significantly in recent years because of that exodus.

The government-affiliated National Coffee Growers' Federation has declined to comment on the moratorium on debt payments, which was agreed unanimously by 650 delegates from nine coffee-growing provinces at Wednesday's meeting in the western city of Pereira.

But some industry analysts say that by throwing down the gauntlet, and saying they have nothing to lose but bad debts and their farms, coffee growers were simply owning up to the grim realities of a country that is unlikely to maintain its annual production of 12 to 13 million 60-kilo bags of coffee much longer.
"The trend in Colombia is clear. We go to 8 million (60-kg) bags," a Bogota-based private coffee exporter said.
The exporter, a leading player in the local market who asked not to be identified, said he sees the crop in Colombia's 1996-97 coffee year totalling no more than 10 million 60-kilo bags.
He said his estimate, a full 2.5 bags less than the Federation's forcecast, was partly due to unusually heavy rains during the flowering period.

But it was also due to the debtor's strike and the abandonment of a growing number of farms by impoverished growers fed up with the insecurity of the countryside and unable to get credit to help fight the plague known as "broca" that has infected more than half of Colombia's coffee plantations.
"The trend is further down," the exporter said of Colombia's production. The bumper days of the 1991-92 coffee year, when Colombia produced up to 18 million 60-kg bags, are long over, he added.
Because of the defiant move by UCN, some industry analysts said the days when National Coffee Growers' Federation ran Colombia's industry almost single-handedly also appeared to be coming to and end.
"What we have here is a revolution, a coffee revolution," one coffee trader said.
He said the UCN, which is also demanding a sharp increase in Colombia's internal coffee price, had every right to do so given the recent run-up in world prices.
"They cannot accept such a gap between international prices and internal prices," he said.
